cse-2014-2-cs-35.approach: Use Rice's theorem for undecidability and a dovetailing simulation to show the language is recursively enumerable.

steps.title: Non-trivial semantic property
steps.body: Membership depends only on $L(M)$: "$L(M)$ contains some string of length 2014". Some TMs have it (one accepting everything), some do not (one accepting nothing). By Rice's theorem, $L$ is **undecidable**.

steps.title: Semi-decide it
steps.body: There are only $2^{2014}$ strings of length 2014. Simulate $M$ on all of them in parallel (dovetailing: one more step on each in every round). If any simulation accepts, accept. If $\langle M\rangle\in L$ this halts and accepts, so $L$ is **recursively enumerable**.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: $L$ is undecidable but recursively enumerable, which is option (B).

Undecidable by Rice; a dovetailed simulation over the $2^{2014}$ strings semi-decides it.
It is RE: the property is "exists an accepted string", which a semi-decider can confirm.
Impossible: every decidable language is recursively enumerable.

pitfalls: Simulating the strings one after another fails: $M$ may loop on the first string and accept a later one, so interleave the runs.

cse-2014-2-cs-36.approach: Relate the occurrences of 110 and 011 to the maximal runs of 1s: they differ only at the ends of the string, so $L_1$ needs finite memory; $L_2$ needs an unbounded counter.

steps.title: Count 110 and 011 via runs of 1s
steps.body: Every occurrence of $110$ ends a maximal run of $\ge 2$ ones that is followed by a $0$; every occurrence of $011$ starts a run of $\ge 2$ ones preceded by a $0$. Each such run strictly inside the string contributes one of each. Only a run touching the start (no $0$ before) or the end (no $0$ after) is unbalanced.

steps.title: $L_1$ is regular
steps.body: So $\#110-\#011\in\{-1,0,1\}$ and depends only on whether the string starts with $11$ and whether it ends with $11$ (with the right neighbours). A DFA remembers the first two symbols and the last two read: finite states. Hence $L_1$ is **regular**.

steps.title: $L_2$ is not regular
steps.body: Runs of 0s and 1s are independent: $0^{a}1^{b}$ has $\max(a-2,0)$ copies of $000$ and $\max(b-2,0)$ copies of $111$. Then $L_2\cap 0^*1^*=\{0^a1^b : \max(a-2,0)\ge \max(b-2,0)\}$, which requires comparing two unbounded counts. Pumping $0^{p+2}1^{p+2}$ inside the $0$-block (decrease $a$) breaks membership, so $L_2$ is **not regular**.

optionAnalysis.reason: $\#110$ and $\#011$ differ by at most 1, decided by the ends of the string; $L_2$ needs counting.
Reversed: $L_2$ is the non-regular one.
$L_2$ is not regular (intersect with $0^*1^*$ and pump).
$L_1$ is regular.

pitfalls: Both definitions look like "compare two counts", but the two patterns in $L_1$ are tied to the same runs, so only one is truly unbounded.
